Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "FGF-signaling is compartmentalized within the mesenchyme and controls proliferation during salamander limb development" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Marianne Bronner (Senior Editor), a Reviewing Editor, and two reviewers.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

Essential revisions:

1) Please break the Discussion section into subsections, including one that compares the findings in axolotl with chick and mouse.

2) Please add a table that compares limb development in axolotl with mouse/chick.

3) Please try, if possible, within a reasonable time frame, to address the reviewer comments below, though some were deemed non-essential (e.g. scRNAseq of limb ectoderm; re-imaging the immunofluorescence). If you cannot address certain comments, please explain why.

Reviewer #1:

In this revised submission, Purushothaman et al., compare limb development in the axolotl salamander to classical findings in chicken and mouse embryos. Some findings confirmed previous studies using more refined techniques, other findings were new. Most striking were the numerous differences seen in axolotl including pre-axial condensation, condensation first along the metapterygial axis, lack of a morphological AER, lack of AER-FGF expression (instead found at the distal mesenchyme), no requirement for FGF signaling for Prox./Distal patterning or cell death, anterior expression of Shh, requirement of Shh for distal proliferation but not cell death. These observations are carefully presented and clearly discussed and very interesting, however, Although the authors responded to many of the criticisms in the first round with additional experiments, I am conflicted as to whether this is a collection of interesting descriptive phenomena vs. a comprehensive mechanistic conceptual advance in the field.

Essential revisions:

1) It would be nice to see some RNA-ISH that is positive in the overlying ectoderm just to rule out the possibility that lack of staining is not due simply to a technical problem with doing RNA-ISH on axolotl ectoderm (some permeability problem). Another method would be to do RNA-ISH on a section.

2) Please show Fgf4 RNA-ISH and other 'data not shown' such as cell death assays even if not very high.

3) How come only scSeq in mesenchyme is shown? Could an analysis of the ectoderm be included? In no FGF ligands detected in this data set, this would be nice to report.

4) Lysotracker and TUNEL are coincident in mouse/chick. Are they in axolotol? Could cells be dying but this is not visible due to failure of phagocytic bodies?

5) The second paragraph of the Discussion section does a better job at summarizing the paper than Abstract, perhaps the abstract could be enhanced with some of the ideas here.

6) Even for the limb bud aficionado it would be useful to have a chart comparing mouse/chick results to findings in axolotl.

7) In Figure 5H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 panel F, I can't tell which of the red patches are positive above background. Also, in the mid-sagittal slice the control limb bud shows almost all cells as positive, is this correct?

8) Why are Christensen et al., 2002; Han et al., 2001 incorrect in their observation of FGF expression in the AER?

Reviewer #2:

The authors are to be congratulated for the quality and scope of the revised manuscript. It is a rigorous and extremely thorough study. All of my concerns have been addressed satisfactorily.

The DiI results are quite interesting. They injected DiI into the early Shh domain of the limb bud and then let it grow, examining the localization of labeled cells at different stages. This allowed them to map the spatiotemporal movements of the initial Shh domain and to determine whether the putative ZPA cells end up in the digits (and if so, which digits). This was very informative. Relative to chick and mouse, axolotl limbs have somewhat crazy fingers and gene expression patterns, but this experiment identifies a deeply conserved feature – the contribution of Shh-expressing cells to the posterior digit(s).

Expansion of the FGF analysis to include all of the Fgfs expressed in the AER of amniotes (FGF 4, 8, 9, 17) as well as Fgf10 and Fgfr1 and Fgfr2, provides definitive evidence that the "AER Fgfs" of amniotes are expressed in the mesoderm of axolotl limb buds (with the possible exception of Fgf4, which was variable but never in the ectoderm). This is an unequivocal demonstration that axolotl limb buds lack the ectodermal domains of Fgfs that are found in the AER of amniotes.

The authors note that the proximal-distal segregation of FGF ligand and receptor expression is puzzling, but the results are clear. Moreover, the in situ hybridization patterns are validated by the scRNAseq data. It is also interesting to see that where Fgfr1 does extend into the distal domain, it is either in or near the cells expressing FGF ligands.

I am impressed by the manner in which the authors responded to the reviewers' criticism that some conclusions were overly broad in the previous version of the paper. Rather than just removing conclusions that were not entirely supported by the results, they investigated whether those conclusions would stand up to further testing. In some places, they were just a half step away from having data that would address the question, but in other cases, they went to great lengths to carry out the appropriate experiments. Where the results provided clear support for the hypothesis (e.g., the AER Fgfs are expressed in the mesenchyme of axolotls), they say so, and where more than one interpretation is possible, they provide conservative conclusions and acknowledge the open questions that remain. I very much like this version of the paper and think that it will be a valuable contribution of the fields of limb development and limb evo-devo, and it will provide important developmental context for regenerative studies.

results.result: Axolotl limb skeletal development exhibits preaxial dominance with uncoupled digit specification and differentiation. Cartilage condensations form proximal-to-distal and anterior-to-posterior (C13, C14), with digits I and II differentiating simultaneously (C15). However, Sox9 expression reveals digit specification occurs in a 2>1>3>4 sequence in 86.66% of limbs (C16), indicating specification precedes and differs from differentiation patterns (C17).
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C17 are well-supported by complementary Alcian blue staining and Sox9 expression data (Figure 1D-E). The quantification (13/15 limbs, 86.66%) provides statistical rigor. The conclusion that specification and differentiation are uncoupled is logically derived from the divergent temporal patterns observed.

results.result: Shh expression in axolotl limbs is posteriorly restricted but proximally localized and appears after Hoxd11 expression. Shh was first detected at stage 45 posteriorly (C18) and persisted through stage 49 in a posterior-proximal position (C19), appearing after Hoxd11 unlike in other tetrapods (C20). An anterior Shh domain was observed at stages 46-48 (C21, C22). The posterior Shh domain remains proximal and does not extend into the autopod (C25), contrasting with the elongated distal expression in other tetrapods.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C25 are supported by in situ hybridization and qRT-PCR data (Figures 2A, 2—figure supplement 2-3). The 42% similarity between Shh and Ihh probes (C23) raises potential cross-reactivity concerns, but distinct Ihh expression patterns (C24) validate probe specificity. The temporal and spatial differences from other tetrapods are well-documented with appropriate citations.

results.result: Shh-expressing cells contribute exclusively to digit IV in axolotl limbs. DiI labeling showed cells from the Shh domain migrated along the posterior margin to form digit IV (C26), similar to chick ZPA cell fate mapping (C27).
results.evaluation: Claim C26 is supported by DiI labeling experiments (Figure 2E, n=34). The comparison to chick experiments (C27) appropriately contextualizes the finding. However, the authors acknowledge that nearby non-Shh-expressing cells were also labeled, introducing some uncertainty about exclusive Shh+ cell contribution.

results.result: AER-specific Fgf ligands and receptors are expressed entirely in the mesenchyme of axolotl limbs, not in the ectoderm. Fgf8, Fgf9, and Fgf17 showed mesenchymal-only expression (C28), while Fgf4 was barely detectable (C29). Fgf receptors FgfR1 and FgfR2 were also mesenchymal (C38-C41). This represents a fundamental departure from the ectodermal-mesenchymal compartmentalization seen in anurans and amniotes (C44).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C44 are strongly supported by comprehensive in situ hybridization data (Figure 3) and validated by single-cell RNA-seq analysis. The use of ectodermal markers (Keratin5, Keratin17) and mesenchymal markers (Msx2) in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 provides critical validation of tissue compartment identification. This is a major finding that challenges established models.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis reveals spatial segregation of Fgf ligands and receptors along the proximodistal axis. PC3 models the proximodistal axis (C45) with proximal and distal markers on opposite ends (C46). Fgf ligands localize distally while receptors localize proximally (C48, C49), with statistical confirmation of separation (C50, p=0.0038). Limited co-expression occurs between FgfR1 and some Fgf ligands (C51), but FgfR2-4 show minimal co-expression with Fgf ligands (C52).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C52 are supported by rigorous computational analysis of published scRNA-seq data (Figure 4). The statistical validation (Welch t-test, p=0.0038) strengthens the conclusion. However, the small sample size (<200 cells, acknowledged by authors) and reliance on a single dataset limit generalizability. The co-expression analysis (C51-C52) suggests some complexity in ligand-receptor interactions that warrants further investigation.

results.result: Fgf-signaling regulates cell proliferation but not cell survival during axolotl limb development. SU5402 treatment from stage 39 resulted in significantly smaller limbs at stage 46 (C53, p<0.0001) with 83% reduction in proliferating cells (C64, p<0.05) but no cell death (C62, C63). Long-term treatment resulted in smaller limbs lacking digit IV in 73.5% of cases (C67, C68). Fgf-signaling regulates Gremlin1 (C72) but Shh-signaling remains relatively independent of Fgf-signaling (C73, C60).
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C73 are well-supported by comprehensive pharmacological inhibition experiments with appropriate statistical analyses (Figure 5). The use of multiple readouts (limb size, gene expression, proliferation, cell death, skeletal phenotypes) provides strong convergent evidence. The statistical correction showing body length changes don't account for limb size differences (C55) strengthens the conclusion. However, SU5402 is a broad FgfR inhibitor, so specific receptor contributions cannot be determined.

results.result: Shh-signaling regulates Fgf8 expression and controls distal cell proliferation during axolotl limb development. Cyclopamine treatment resulted in significantly smaller limbs at stage 46 (C75, p<0.0001) with efficient Shh pathway inhibition (C76). Fgf8 and Gremlin1 expression were significantly reduced (C77, C78), placing them downstream of Shh (C79, C83). Shh inhibition caused 53% reduction in proliferation (C81) with dramatic loss in the distal limb bud (C82) but no cell death (C80).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C84 are supported by cyclopamine inhibition experiments with appropriate controls and statistical validation (Figure 6). The spatial specificity of proliferation defects (distal vs. proportional for Fgf inhibition) provides mechanistic insight. The comparison to Shh-/- mouse phenotypes (C74) appropriately contextualizes findings. However, cyclopamine can have off-target effects, and genetic validation would strengthen conclusions.

results.result: Urodele limb development exhibits unique features distinguishing it from anurans and amniotes. Urodeles show preaxial skeletal differentiation (C1), lack an AER (C2), and demonstrate autonomous development temporally decoupled from body axis patterning (C87). These features contrast with postaxial dominance and AER-dependent development in anurans and amniotes (C6), and urodeles uniquely retain adult limb regeneration capacity (C90).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C6, C85-C90 represent established knowledge appropriately cited and contextualized. These background claims provide essential framework for interpreting the novel findings. The citations appear accurate and the comparisons are well-established in the literature.

results.result: Salamander limbs lack a molecular AER, with AER-specific Fgfs and receptors expressed in mesenchyme, and Fgf-signaling regulating proliferation across all three limb axes rather than cell survival and proximodistal patterning.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 are summary statements directly supported by the detailed experimental results in other claim groups. These represent the core conclusions of the manuscript and are well-supported by the comprehensive data presented.

results.result: Inhibiting Shh-signaling affects multiple aspects of limb development including Fgf8 expression, anteroposterior patterning, and distal cell proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 are summary statements from the abstract that are supported by detailed experimental results presented in later claim groups (particularly C75-C84). These accurately represent the findings.

results.result: The role of Shh-signaling from the ZPA is conserved in salamander limb development, but movement of AER-Fgf ligands to the mesenchyme was accompanied by functional changes in Fgf-signaling regulation. The divergent molecular program in urodeles resides predominantly in the limb mesenchyme.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 represent the major conclusions synthesizing all experimental findings. These are well-supported by the comprehensive data on Shh function (conserved) and Fgf compartmentalization and function (divergent). The conclusions are appropriately cautious and acknowledge both conservation and divergence.
